General anaesthesia for birth: what to expect

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

General anaesthesia makes you unconscious for an operation. Most caesarean births use a spinal or epidural anaesthetic so you can remain awake, but general anaesthesia may be the best option in some circumstances. Needing it is not a failure or a reflection of how well you have coped with labour.

Why the plan may include general anaesthesia

An urgent birth may leave too little time for a spinal or epidural to work. A regional technique may also be unsuitable because of particular medical findings, impossible to place, or insufficient for surgery. Your preferences and previous experiences belong in the discussion too.

General anaesthesia is not routine pain relief for an uncomplicated vaginal birth, although an operation during or after birth can require it. Ask what is recommended, why, and what alternatives are feasible in the time available.

Previous back surgery does not decide everything

Spinal surgery or a curved spine can make placement more challenging, but neither automatically rules out regional anaesthesia. An antenatal anaesthetic consultation, previous operation records and sometimes ultrasound can help the team plan.

Bleeding disorders, blood-thinning medicines, infection and other health conditions also require individualized assessment. Do not stop prescribed medicines yourself to make one anaesthetic option possible. Share allergies, previous anaesthetic difficulties, loose teeth and any relevant family history with the anaesthetist.

Some conditions involving raised pressure inside the skull can make a spinal or epidural unsuitable, but the diagnosis and physiology must be reviewed rather than assuming every brain tumour or previous back operation requires general anaesthesia. In a time-critical emergency, the speed and feasibility of each method also matter.

How the team prepares

Follow the hospital’s instructions about food, drink and medicines before planned surgery. If an emergency occurs after you have eaten, tell the team accurately; they have procedures for managing that situation. You do not need to perform airway manoeuvres yourself.

In theatre, monitors track your condition and medicines are given through a vein. Oxygen is provided before you go to sleep. The anaesthetic team manages your breathing and airway throughout the procedure. A breathing tube helps protect the airway; it is not simply a device that increases the risk of stomach contents entering the lungs.

General anaesthesia combines unconsciousness, pain control and prevention of memory of surgery. Medicines may also relax or temporarily paralyse muscles and reduce the body’s stress responses. A muscle relaxant alone does not provide unconsciousness or pain relief, which is why the complete anaesthetic and monitoring matter.

The team may give medicine to reduce stomach acidity, use a rapid sequence of induction medicines and apply an airway-protection manoeuvre when appropriate. Once asleep, you receive ongoing anaesthetic medicine by inhalation, through a vein or both, with oxygen and supported breathing. Agents such as sevoflurane, isoflurane or desflurane are examples, not a standard recipe for every birth. The breathing tube is usually removed when you can breathe and protect your airway adequately.

Discuss side effects and uncommon risks

A sore throat, nausea, shivering or sleepiness can occur afterwards. More serious problems, such as a severe allergic reaction, difficult airway management or stomach contents reaching the lungs, are uncommon but part of the consent discussion. Your own risk depends on the situation and your health.

Accidental awareness means remembering events when you were intended to be unconscious. It is uncommon, but the risk is higher in obstetric general anaesthesia than in many other operations. If you remember something distressing or think you were aware, tell the team and ask for an anaesthetic review. Your experience should be taken seriously.

Dry mouth and vomiting can accompany the more familiar sore throat, nausea or shivering during recovery. Anaesthetic drugs can also temporarily affect the newborn’s alertness or breathing, depending on the drugs, timing and the reason for urgent birth. The team balances prompt safe delivery with limiting unnecessary exposure and providing neonatal support.

During accidental awareness, a person may be unable to move because a muscle relaxant is still working. Recollections can include sounds, sensations or occasionally pain, and even a brief experience may be distressing. Psychological support and a clear anaesthetic debrief can be offered.

Your baby and birth partner

The neonatal team is available to assess the baby, who may sometimes need breathing support. When both of you are ready, staff can help you meet and hold your baby. Ask beforehand how your birth partner will receive updates and what contact they can have with the baby.

Operating-theatre arrangements vary, and a partner is commonly asked to wait nearby during general anaesthesia. If you miss the first moments, ask the team to explain what happened. A birth debrief can help you make sense of an unexpected or urgent delivery.

Recovery, feeding and support

Pain relief and treatment for nausea should be offered as needed. Tell staff if you remain uncomfortable or unusually drowsy. Have help when holding and caring for the baby until you are sufficiently alert and steady. Do not share a sleep surface with the baby when anaesthetic or sedating medicines may still affect you.

Breastfeeding can usually resume once you are awake, alert and able to feed safely; routine discarding of milk after anaesthesia is generally unnecessary. Ask the team to check the actual medicines used, especially repeated sedating painkillers or if your baby is premature or unwell. If you are separated, request help with expressing and a feeding plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Obstetric anaesthesia guidance uses regional techniques for most caesareans but supports general anaesthesia when urgency, clinical findings or inadequate regional anaesthesia make it appropriate.

Airway protection, full monitoring and supported recovery are the team’s responsibility; awareness concerns and feeding plans deserve individualized follow-up.

How BeMama can help

Discuss previous anaesthetic experiences and medical conditions before birth where possible, and request an explanation and recovery support after an unexpected general anaesthetic.

When to seek help

Do not perform airway manoeuvres yourself; report distressing memories, severe symptoms or unusual drowsiness and obtain help caring for the baby until alert.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Most caesareans use regional anaesthesia, but general anaesthesia is sometimes appropriate.
  • Previous spine surgery does not automatically prevent a spinal or epidural.
  • Discuss your medical history, concerns and preferences with the anaesthetist.
  • Recovery includes pain control, supported baby care and an individualized feeding plan.

Frequently asked questions

Will I always need general anaesthesia after a back operation?

No. The type of surgery, current anatomy and other findings need assessment. A spinal or epidural may still be possible.

Should I press on my own throat as I go to sleep?

No. Airway management is the anaesthetic team’s responsibility. Follow their instructions rather than attempting any manoeuvre yourself.

Do I have to stop breastfeeding afterwards?

Usually not. Feeding generally resumes when you are awake and able to do it safely, with advice about the medicines used and your baby’s health.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
